title: God's number for the Rubik's Cube
hook: Every scrambled Rubik's Cube can be solved in twenty moves or fewer.
peek: A Rubik's Cube has about 43 quintillion possible arrangements. In 2010 a team proved that every one of them can be solved in at most 20 face turns. They needed borrowed Google computer time to check them all.
lede: God's number is the most moves an all-knowing solver would ever need to solve a Rubik's Cube from any scramble. The cube has about 43 quintillion positions, so the answer stayed open for 30 years. In 2010 Tomas Rokicki, Herbert Kociemba, Morley Davidson and John Dethridge proved it is 20, counting any turn of a face as one move.

bullets.text: In 1981 Morwen Thistlethwaite showed that 52 moves are always enough. Over the next three decades, mathematicians pushed that ceiling down step by step until it finally met the floor.
The floor came from positions that really do need 20 moves. The first one proved to need them, in 1995, was the superflip, where every edge is flipped in place and everything else looks solved.
To close the gap, the team split the positions into billions of groups and used symmetry to cut the work. Google donated spare computer time equal to about 35 years on a single processor.
If a half turn counts as two moves, the answer changes. Under that rule God's number was proved in 2014 to be 26.
